Alphabetical listing of school names with their district numbers, page 1.

The first organized school in Kansas was organized in Wyandotte by J.M. Armstrong in 1844. It lasted until his death in 1852. The school had the distinction of being the first established for white children in what is now the state of Kansas. A school for whites was established in Council Grove in 1851 by Mr. T.S. Huffaker. The State of Kansas is challenged to find another county surpassing Jackson in its zealous devotion to educational matters.
Shortly after the county was organized in 1857, the people began to think about schools for their children.

The first school was taught in this county by Miss Hariet Warfield of Clay County Missouri in 1857. It was gotten up on the subscription plan, and held in a little log cabin, 10 feet square, located on the SW 1/4 section 23, township 9, range 16. This would put about 5 miles east of Hoyt. (1)
School was started in Jefferson township the same year. Mrs. H.S. Hart held school in her log cabin.
Hard times, drought, the coming of the Civil War and the internal strife in Kansas kept the people of Jackson County from doing much about schools until after 1861. (1)

The first real school was built in the county in 1858. It was built out of logs and was also used as a church. Information from the Kansas State Historical Society, says that the lighting came from leaving out one log in the wall on one side. It was heated by a fireplace. It was taught by Miss Anna Parrot. The name of it was called Brick, and was also the first organized district in county. Permission for this was granted on June 20, 1859. It was located on land which was part of the Pottawatomie Reserve. The school term was six months, three months in spring and three in the fall.

In 1868, George and Mary Hafer donated one acre of land to the school. It was about 1/2 mile west of the log cabin. In the same Brick school was built. In one porch was W.H. Webster. He taught for seven terms. At one time there were 58 students. The building was also used as a church until a church building was completed in 1890. In 1916 the second building was torn down and a building, with a basement was erected. School was held here until it was destroyed by a tornado in 1962. The last teacher was Katherin Linehan.
(The information about Brick was Kansas Historical Society and Forest Morris family and the Everett Gibson family.)
The first school in Douglas township was built in 1859. It was a
log structure, 18x20 constructed by neighbors who worked together and did an agreed part of the work. Later

was built. A group of people met Nov. S, 1859 to organize district #12. They chose the site on March 17, 1860. This located in the SE corner 1/4 of section 22, township 9, range 16. Bainbridge, RichardS and Rippitoe were names frequently mentioned.

The first school in Jefferson was taught by Mrs. H.S. Hart. Ed Hulan taught the first one in Grant township in 1858 and the first building was built in 1859. Sophia Lattimer taught the first one in Liberty township in a log house on the subscription plan. James B. Hastings was the first teacher in Straight Creek and the first building was erected in 1859.
The first school in Tippinville was taught by Miss Rioce in the winter of 1857 and 1858 in her home. One source says the building was bout 1/4 mile east of the crossroads.

Alan Gardnier states the first building made of logs, was built where the cemetery south of Denison is. A few years later a school house was built on the Claud Braum shop lots where Denison now stands.

A Log building housed the first one in Cedar township. It was built by individual subscription on S.J. Elliot's land in 1858. It later moved 1 mile south. The next was built in 1862. ( from Platt Book 1881 Cedar township. )

There were at least 14 school districts formed in 1859. They were Brick, Holton, Denison, Center, Stone (it was called Banner later), Liberty, Philo, Pleasant Valley, Lawn Ridge, Mulinax, Cedar Hill, North Star, Point Pleasant, Cedar Vale.
